transcript:
Meeting header: Date: 2025-07-15 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~52m | Attendees: Sarah Park (Redwood AE), Tom Nguyen (Redwood SE), Lina Morales (BlueNova Head of ML), Raj Iyer (BlueNova CTO), Ana Gomez (BlueNova Procurement)

Auto-summary (auto-gen, may be noisy): Discussed POC success criteria (latency SLOs, throughput targets, acceptable error/hallucination rates), workload sizing (avg tokens, concurrency), benchmark plan (throughput, 95th pctl latency, cold vs hot cache), pilot commercial guardrails (credit allocation, trial terms), and procurement path (SOW/MSA, expected timelines). Next steps: Redwood to share credits + draft SOW; SE to run bench.

00:00:03 Sarah Park: hey everyone, thanks for making time, quick intro, I'm Sarah, AE on this account. Today's goal is to align on POC success criteria and the commercial guardrails so procurement can see the runway.
00:00:15 Lina Morales: great, hi all, Lina here. we've got a fairly tight window to prove latency and cost — our execs want numbers within a couple weeks.
00:00:28 Raj Iyer: yeah hi, raj, CTO. key thing for us is can you hit 200ms p95 on our chat flows, and what's the expected token cost, like rough order.
00:00:40 Tom Nguyen: (SE) hey team, Tom here. we usually recommend starting with a baseline run — a 50-user concurrent workload with your typical prompt mix, run for 30 minutes to measure steady-state throughput and p95, then a few spike tests.
00:00:55 Ana Gomez: also procurement things — we need a pilot credit number and outline of terms, e.g., how long is the pilot, what happens if we go over credits, any liability limits.
00:01:10 Sarah Park: perfect. to frame it: typical Redwood pilot has two parts — an evaluation bench + commercial credits for usage. We can offer a credits allocation and a 45- to 60-day pilot term normally, but we can flex based on scope.
00:01:28 Lina Morales: can you give examples of credit sizing? like do you give dollar credits or token credits?
00:01:36 Sarah Park: we provide a credits sheet that maps to estimated token usage and reserved throughput for the bench runs. for example, a small pilot might be $7k of credits (roughly X tokens at hosted pricing) and a medium pilot $25k. we can also allocate a dedicated short-lived t-shirt-sized dedicated pool for benchmarking if needed.
00:01:57 Tom Nguyen: important caveat — dedicated pools carry a setup time and minimum commit for Dedicated; for a short pilot we usually emulate dedicated performance on hosted with pinned model variants + priority routing. that avoids infra lead time.
00:02:15 Raj Iyer: so for our SLA ask — 200ms p95 — is that realistic on hosted or do we need dedicated?
00:02:24 Tom Nguyen: depends on model and token length. for a Llama-derivative 13B quantized and a typical 60-token response, we've seen sub-200ms p95 on dedicated; on hosted with optimizations you can approach 200ms but it's not guaranteed under bursty concurrency. part of the bench will be to show the delta.
00:02:44 Lina Morales: our average response token length is 80 tokens and prompts average 40 tokens, we expect 30 qps steady, peak 120 qps.
00:02:54 Tom Nguyen: ok that's helpful — we'll size bench cluster to mimic 120 qps peaks and 30 qps sustained. we'll run both cold-start and warmed cache tests to show the impact of KV/prefix caching.
00:03:09 Ana Gomez: and what about data handling — do you store logs? does that count against credits? we need to know from security side.
00:03:19 Sarah Park: good Q. by default hosted logs for debugging are retained short-term; persistent logs and extended retention are add-ons. Credits cover inference tokens and standard telemetry; storage or long-term retention is outside and will be itemized in SOW. we'll include that in the credit mapping doc.
00:03:36 Raj Iyer: procurement will ask about SOC2 and ISO — we need the security pack.
00:03:42 Sarah Park: yes, we'll send the security pack (SOC2, ISO27001 summary, encryption/KMS details, and network diagrams). note: doc auto-names sometimes show S0C2 in transcripts, so ignore typos.
00:03:55 Tom Nguyen: back to benchmarks — recommended metrics: 95th pctl latency, 50th pctl, throughput (req/s), tokens/sec, cost per 1k responses, and accuracy/regression against your golden set (we'll need 200 labeled examples).
00:04:13 Lina Morales: accuracy — what metric? perplexity isn't helpful for us. we want recall on entity extraction and false-positive rate for hallucination.
00:04:22 Tom Nguyen: understood. we'll define evaluation metrics with you: entity F1, hallucination rate (measured by manual review on sample outputs), and end-to-end response time. we'll include a small human eval plan.
00:04:37 Raj Iyer: timeline — how long from SOW to bench results?
00:04:42 Sarah Park: typical is: SOW + credit agreement signed -> infra & bench config in 3–5 business days -> bench run over 2–3 days -> results and analysis within 2 business days after runs. so roughly two weeks end-to-end after SOW.
00:04:57 Ana Gomez: procurement lead times for us are usually 4–6 weeks for legal + PO. we need to understand if the pilot can start before the legal is finished.
00:05:06 Sarah Park: yes, we can do a conditional pilot start with an MOA (memorandum of agreement) or a simple pilot order form that includes the credit terms and limited liability and asserts a future MSA. it's common to run the technical pilot in parallel to contracting with limited-risk terms.
00:05:22 Lina Morales: what about overages? if we exceed credits during bench runs because of more iterations, do you bill or throttle?
00:05:29 Sarah Park: two options: we can set hard caps that throttle when credits exhausted, or soft caps with overage billing at discounted pilot rates. we'll propose both so you can pick.
00:05:39 Tom Nguyen: practically, for bench stability we often set a hard cap and send alerts; for customer explorations a soft-overage model is more flexible but requires PO pre-approval.
00:05:52 Raj Iyer: would Redwood provide a cost model for working production — like cost per 1M tokens across various quantizations?
00:05:59 Sarah Park: yes, Optimize team can produce a cost breakdown by model size, quantization level, and batching configs. that's separate from pilot credits but we'll include a representative slide in the pack.
00:06:12 Lina Morales: are there any constraints on using our PII data in the pilot? we need assured non-retention for certain fields.
00:06:21 Tom Nguyen: you can use PII if you opt for private deployment or VPC with customer-managed keys; for hosted pilot we recommend token scrubbing or synthetic data unless you sign the data addendum. we'll highlight options in the security pack.
00:06:36 Ana Gomez: on procurement logistics: what's the minimal paperwork we can do to get the bench started? a short pilot order form would be ideal.
00:06:44 Sarah Park: we can do a one-page pilot order: scope, credits, term (45 days), basic liability cap, and acceptance criteria. legal can later fold that into an MSA + SOW if you move forward.
00:06:56 Raj Iyer: acceptance criteria — let's be explicit: p95 latency <= 220ms for 80-token responses under 30 qps sustained, throughput >= 900 resp/min sustained, hallucination rate < 3% on entity extraction. does that sound measurable?
00:07:12 Tom Nguyen: yes that's measurable. we'll instrument bench to capture those metrics. a quick note: p95 can vary with prompt length and model; we'll run a sensitivity analysis and show trade-offs.
00:07:24 Lina Morales: also add a quality gating rule: if hallucination increases > 1% vs baseline we consider that a regression.
00:07:30 Tom Nguyen: noted. we'll baseline against your current model and provide diffing.
00:07:36 Sarah Park: commercial guardrail question — for pilot credits, do you prefer to see it as a capped dollar amount or as a set of reserved runs?
00:07:44 Ana Gomez: procurement wants predictable buck numbers. dollar credits are easier.
00:07:48 Raj Iyer: engineering wants reserved runs to guarantee throughput. maybe a hybrid?
00:07:52 Sarah Park: exactly — hybrid is common: dollar credits for general use + a short reserved benchmarking window (a reserved capacity slot for 2–4 hours) to hit peak throughput. we'll reflect that in the pilot sheet.
00:08:05 Lina Morales: what's the estimated cost for running a 120 qps peak bench for 2 hours?
00:08:11 Tom Nguyen: rough calc: depends on model; let's ballpark $800–1,500 for hosted optimized 13B runs; if we emulate dedicated performance you add a small dedicated reservation surcharge. we'll give exact numbers once we size with your prompt specifics.
00:08:25 Ana Gomez: if costs are high, is there an academic discount? noi, just kidding — but can we get a one-time pilot discount?
00:08:31 Sarah Park: pilot credits already tend to be discounted vs list; for expansion we'll negotiate committed tiers.
00:08:38 Raj Iyer: any vendor lock-in concerns? can we export KV cache or checkpoint?
00:08:44 Tom Nguyen: KV caches are runtime artifacts and not exportable; model weights depend on licensing. for evals you can export logs and outputs for your offline analysis.
00:08:55 Lina Morales: ok. technical deep-dive question — when you say warmed cache tests, what's the warmup policy?
00:09:01 Tom Nguyen: we run a prefix load to populate KV caches and then run steady-state traffic. we'll document warmup sequences; sometimes the warmup time is 10–30m depending on sequence lengths.
00:09:13 Sarah Park: quick procurement note: we've worked with finance teams to accept pilot credits as a one-time invoice or a PO. we can be flexible to match your process.
00:09:23 Ana Gomez: good to know. we prefer PO + invoice.
00:09:26 Sarah Park: noted.
00:09:29 00:09:30 (crosstalk)
00:09:36 Tom Nguyen: on measurement — we'll run 3 categories: functional correctness (F1, hallucination), performance (p50/p95/p99, through put), and cost (tokens, cost/response). we'll produce a bench report with charts and recommendations (batching, quant, routing).
00:09:56 Raj Iyer: what's the rollback path if we see poor perf in pilot?
00:10:01 Sarah Park: canary fallback is a feature: route to a fallback smaller model or API-based fallback. for the pilot, we can leave that as an operational mitigation but it's more of a production control.
00:10:12 Lina Morales: what about contractually defining success — who signs off?
00:10:16 Ana Gomez: procurement will require a named sign-off from Lina for technical acceptance and from Raj or VP for business acceptance. that should be in SOW.
00:10:26 Sarah Park: we'll include explicit sign-off criteria in the SOW: metric thresholds, sample size, and date.
00:10:31 Tom Nguyen: logistics for bench — we'll need a small harness: a set of runner scripts, your prompt templates, and expected labels. we can provide the harness and you can run it in your VPC or we can run it from Redwood infra — both ok.
00:10:45 Lina Morales: if Redwood runs the bench, how do we share the sample data securely?
00:10:50 Sarah Park: prefer S3 presigned links or SFTP with key-based auth; for sensitive fields use tokenization. we'll include our upload SOP.
00:10:58 Raj Iyer: curious — any hidden fees like GPU spin-up or provisioning costs during pilot?
00:11:04 Sarah Park: no hidden fees; credits cover compute + tokens for the pilot according to mapping. dedicated hardware incurs a temporary reservation fee which we'll call out.
00:11:12 Ana Gomez: about the legal — if we sign an MOA to start pilot can we include a clause that the MOA is non-binding beyond pilot so procurement can continue to review MSA?
00:11:22 Sarah Park: yes, standard practice. MOA covers pilot scope, credits, term, and limited indemnity; full commercial terms are finalized in the MSA.
00:11:31 Lina Morales: what about audit logs — we need request-level traceability for debug and for security.
00:11:36 Tom Nguyen: console exposes request IDs, per-token cost, latency breakdowns; for Private deployments you get full audit logs forwarded to your SIEM. we'll detail retention options.
00:11:48 Sarah Park: ok let's zoom into the POC acceptance criteria recapped: 1) p95 latency <= 220ms under 30 qps sustained for 80-token responses; 2) throughput >= 900 resp/min; 3) hallucination rate < 3% and regression < 1% vs baseline; 4) bench reproducible run with charts and raw logs.
00:12:10 Raj Iyer: agree with those, want to add a cost per response threshold: <$0.015 per response at pilot config.
00:12:17 Sarah Park: noted — we'll estimate cost per response as part of bench.
00:12:21 Lina Morales: timeline recap?
00:12:24 Sarah Park: immediate next steps: Sarah sends pilot credit sheet + security pack + draft short-form MOA by 2025-07-17. Tom to provision bench infra and propose bench schedule (3 day window) by 2025-07-22. BlueNova to send prompts + 200 eval examples by 2025-07-18. Procurement to confirm PO path and lead reviewers by 2025-07-25.
00:12:42 Ana Gomez: sounds good. I'll confirm procurement approvers.
00:12:46 Raj Iyer: can we lock a benchmarking window week of 2025-07-28?
00:12:51 Tom Nguyen: tentative yes — will propose 2025-07-28 to 2025-07-30 window; final once we have prompts.
00:12:58 Lina Morales: one last question on guardrails — if the bench shows we need Dedicated to meet latency, will pilot credits apply toward commitment?
00:13:07 Sarah Park: yes, pilot credits can be credit toward an initial Dedicated commitment within a defined timeframe. we'll make that explicit in the pilot sheet.
00:13:15 00:13:17 (brief pause)
00:13:20 Tom Nguyen: technical note — please include some high-latency outlier prompts, like past-tense long documents, so we measure worst-case.
00:13:29 Lina Morales: will do.
00:13:31 Sarah Park: ok wrapping — recap of decisions made: acceptance metrics agreed (latency/throughput/quality/cost), pilot term tentatively 45 days, hybrid credit + reserved benchmarking window, pilot can start with MOA before MSA, next steps and owners as we listed.
00:13:50 Raj Iyer: thanks, appreciate the clarity.
00:13:53 Ana Gomez: thanks everyone.
00:13:55 Sarah Park: adjourn — Sarah to send docs. Bye.

Post-meeting notes (auto): Possible follow-on: Dedicated eval if hosted can't meet p95; procurement will request MOA/PO. SE to include baseline comparisons to current in-house model.
